chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from Ammar al-Sabati, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What do you say about a group of people who were traveling and walking on the shore of the sea, when they found a dead man naked whom the sea had cast up? They were naked, having only an izār (loincloth) or a ridā’ (garment) on them. How do they pray over him while they are naked, with no surplus garment to shroud him with?

He (peace be upon him) said: 'A grave is dug for him, and he is placed in his grave (lahd). A brick is placed over his private part, so he is covered by the brick and the stone. Then the funeral prayer is prayed over him, and then he is buried.'

I said: So the funeral prayer is not prayed over him after he is buried? He said: 'The funeral prayer is not prayed over the dead after he is buried, nor is it prayed over him while he is naked until his private part is covered.'

key_terms.عَوْرَة: Private part or area that must be covered
key_terms.لَحْد: A grave with a niche or recess on one side, typical in Shia jurisprudence

ai.seo_question: How is the funeral prayer performed if there is insufficient cloth to shroud the entire body of the deceased?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the practical jurisprudence of *salat al-janazah* when burial shrouds are scarce, specifically in a scenario where mourners themselves are nearly naked. It establishes that covering the *awrah* (private parts) is the essential condition for the validity of the prayer, permitting the use of bricks or stones as a valid substitute for fabric. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the necessity of modesty (*haya*) even in death, ensuring the deceased is not exposed during the ritual prayer.
